title: On the Possibility of Informative Equilibria in Futures Markets with Feedback
journal: Journal of the European Economic Association
abstract: Abstract We study the existence of equilibria and the information content of prices in futures markets where the probability of future payoffs can be altered by an intervening agent who acts in response to the market price, hence creating a feedback effect. We focus on the market with the simplest possible structure: traders betting on the occurrence of a future event by buying or selling Arrow-Debreu securities (one dollar claims contingent on a binary outcome). We find that in the presence of feedback: (i) a rational expectations equilibrium may not exist; (ii) the market price may decline in response to information that is ex-ante more favorable to the occurrence of the underlying event; (iii) an equilibrium that reveals no information may obtain. Thus, feedback from an intervening agent materially alters the way in which price responds to information, and potentially undermines the viability of the market itself.
summary_en: When prices in a futures market reflect both fundamental information and traders' beliefs about each other's information, can the resulting equilibrium prices remain informative about underlying fundamentals? Lieli and Nieto-Barthaburu show that — contra some classical results — informative equilibria are possible when traders' loss functions are sufficiently asymmetric. They characterise the conditions: heterogeneity in trader preferences must dominate the feedback effect through which prices distort each trader's information. The result reopens the door to using futures prices as predictors of fundamentals in markets where the no-trade theorem would otherwise rule out informative pricing.
data_used: Theoretical model — equilibrium analysis of futures markets with heterogeneous-loss traders and feedback between prices and information.
policy_relevance: MNB and Hungarian energy regulator MEKH use futures prices (interest-rate futures, electricity futures, FX futures) as predictors of underlying fundamentals when designing policy. The paper provides theoretical conditions under which futures prices retain informational content — relevant for MNB's interest-rate signal-extraction methodology and MEKH's electricity-market analysis.
